questions.question_text: A patient is to receive $1.5$ L of fluid over $6$ hours through a drip giving $12$ drops/mL. How many drops per minute are required?

options.why: Left the time in hours instead of converting $6$ h to $360$ min.
Found the volume rate in mL/min but never multiplied by the $12$ drops/mL.
Divided by the $12$ drops/mL instead of multiplying, inverting one link of the chain.

questions.solution_text:
$\dfrac{\text{drops}}{\text{time}} = \dfrac{\text{drops}}{\text{volume}} \times \dfrac{\text{volume}}{\text{time}}$
$= \dfrac{12\text{ drops}}{1\text{ mL}} \times \dfrac{1500\text{ mL}}{360\text{ min}}$
$= \dfrac{12 \times 1500}{360}$
$= 50$
The rate is $50$ drops/min.

questions.question_text: A machine fills $30$ bottles per minute, and each bottle holds $250$ mL. How long will the machine take to bottle $600$ L of juice?

options.why: Treated each bottle as a full litre, dividing $600$ by the $30$ bottles/min without using the $250$ mL capacity.
Converted $600$ L to $60\,000$ mL instead of $600\,000$ mL, a factor-of-ten slip.
Found the fill rate as $750$ mL/min instead of $30 \times 250 = 7500$ mL/min, dropping a factor of ten.

questions.solution_text:
$\dfrac{\text{time}}{\text{volume}} = \dfrac{\text{time}}{\text{bottles}} \times \dfrac{\text{bottles}}{\text{volume}}$
$= \dfrac{1\text{ min}}{30\text{ bottles}} \times \dfrac{1\text{ bottle}}{250\text{ mL}}$
$= \dfrac{1\text{ min}}{7500\text{ mL}}$
$600$ L $= 600\,000$ mL
$x = \dfrac{600\,000}{7500}$
$= 80$ min
It takes $1$ h $20$ min.

questions.question_text: A car uses $8.2$ L of fuel per $100$ km. Fuel costs $\$1.85$ per litre. What is the fuel cost per kilometre?

options.why: Stopped at the cost per $100$ km without dividing by $100$ to reach one kilometre.
Divided $\$1.85$ by $8.2$ instead of multiplying the two rates together.
Divided the $8.2$ L by the price per litre, chaining the rates in the wrong order.

questions.question_text: Tropical fish breed at a rate of $8$ new fry every $2$ days per female fish. With $9$ female fish, how long does it take to produce $90$ new fry?

options.why: Used the rate for one fish only, forgetting to multiply it by the $9$ female fish.
Read the rate as $8$ fry per day per fish instead of $8$ every two days.
Multiplied the time by $9$ instead of multiplying the rate, scaling in the wrong direction.

questions.solution_text:
Rate per fish: $\dfrac{8\text{ fry}}{2\text{ days}} = \dfrac{4\text{ fry}}{1\text{ day}}$
Rate for $9$ fish: $\dfrac{4\text{ fry}}{1\text{ day}} \times 9 = \dfrac{36\text{ fry}}{1\text{ day}}$
$\dfrac{36\text{ fry}}{1\text{ day}} = \dfrac{90\text{ fry}}{x\text{ days}}$
$x = \dfrac{90}{36}$
$= 2.5$
It takes $2.5$ days.

questions.question_text: A $20$ kg bag of chicken feed costs $\$16.40$ and a hen eats $120$ g of feed per day. What does the calculation $\dfrac{16.40}{20\,000} \times 120$ find?

options.text: The cost of the feed one hen eats in a day
The number of days one bag of feed lasts a hen
options.why: That would be $20\,000 \div 120$; this expression has dollars, not grams, on top.

options.text: The mass of feed a hen eats in a day
options.why: The $120$ g is already given; multiplying it by a dollars-per-gram rate gives a cost.

options.text: The cost of $1$ kg of feed
options.why: That would be $\$16.40 \div 20$; this expression scales all the way down to one day's feed.

questions.solution_text:
$\dfrac{\$16.40}{20\,000\text{ g}} \times \dfrac{120\text{ g}}{1\text{ day}}$
The units are $\dfrac{\$}{\text{g}} \times \dfrac{\text{g}}{\text{day}}$, and the grams cancel to leave $\dfrac{\$}{\text{day}}$.
It finds the cost of the feed one hen eats in a day, about $\$0.10$.

questions.question_text: A patient needs $0.75$ g of medicine per day. Pills contain $125$ mg each and cost $75$ c per pill. What is the annual cost of the medicine, using a $365$-day year?

options.why: Costed one pill per day, ignoring that $0.75$ g needs six $125$ mg pills.
Gave the number of pills used in a year rather than multiplying by the price per pill.
Stopped at the daily cost without multiplying by the $365$ days in the year.

questions.solution_text:
$\dfrac{\text{cost}}{\text{time}} = \dfrac{\text{medicine}}{\text{time}} \times \dfrac{\text{pills}}{\text{medicine}} \times \dfrac{\text{cost}}{\text{pill}}$
$= \dfrac{750\text{ mg}}{1\text{ day}} \times \dfrac{1\text{ pill}}{125\text{ mg}} \times \dfrac{\$0.75}{1\text{ pill}}$
$= \dfrac{\$4.50}{1\text{ day}}$
$= \dfrac{\$4.50 \times 365}{1\text{ year}}$
$= \dfrac{\$1642.50}{1\text{ year}}$

questions.question_text: What is the drip rate per minute for $2.6$ L of fluid over $6$ hours with a drip size giving $12$ drops/mL? Answer to the nearest drop.

options.why: Found the volume rate of $7.2$ mL/min but never multiplied by the $12$ drops/mL.
Truncated $86.6$ instead of rounding to the nearest whole drop.
Divided by the $6$ hours without converting the time to $360$ minutes.

questions.solution_text:
$2.6$ L $= 2600$ mL
$\dfrac{\text{drops}}{\text{time}} = \dfrac{\text{drops}}{\text{volume}} \times \dfrac{\text{volume}}{\text{time}}$
$= \dfrac{12\text{ drops}}{1\text{ mL}} \times \dfrac{2600\text{ mL}}{360\text{ min}}$
$= \dfrac{12 \times 2600}{360}$
$= 86.6\ldots$
The rate is $87$ drops/min.
